History

Rolling papers began in Alcoy, Spain, in the 1500s, where smokers wrapped salvaged cigar tobacco in paper scraps; dedicated paper factories followed in the town in the mid-1700s, and a Spanish monk is credited with the first folded booklet around 1765. The trade spread through France and Spain in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries: Zig-Zag traces its origins to France in 1879, introduced interleaved booklets in 1894, and trademarked the name in 1906. RAW launched its first unbleached papers in 2005. Papers were first made for tobacco; cannabis smokers adopted the same sheets, and makers later offered hemp, rice, and flax papers aimed at them. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. Museums, trade guides, and manufacturer manuals preserve the steps of that change, and the sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage. The history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day. The form changed slowly, through small improvements in materials and manufacturing rather than sudden reinvention, and each improvement can be traced in the sources cited at the end of this record. What stayed constant was the job itself, and what changed was how reliably, how evenly, and how durably that job could be done with ordinary materials and ordinary tools.

The supply in detail

The rolling papers works by a thin sheet of plant-fibre paper with a gum strip along one edge is wrapped around ground herb, sealed by moistening the gum, and the resulting cylinder is lit at one end and drawn from the other. It is made from hemp, rice, flax, or wood-pulp paper, 10 to 14 gsm, with a gum arabic adhesive strip, and a common example measures 1 1/4 size 78 mm x 44 mm; king size 110 mm x 44 mm; booklets of 32 leaves are common. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Hemp, rice, flax, or wood-pulp paper at about 10 to 14 grams per square metre; gum arabic adhesive strip along one long edge

Dimensions: Single wide 70 mm x 36 mm; 1 1/4 size 78 mm x 44 mm; 1 1/2 size 78 mm x 60 mm; King size 110 mm x 44 mm; King slim 110 mm x 53 mm

Mechanism: Ground herb is spread along the paper, the paper is rolled into a cylinder, the gum strip is moistened and pressed to seal the seam, and the finished roll is lit at the tip and drawn from the filter end

Use: Place a filter tip at one end, spread ground herb evenly, roll the paper into a cylinder, lick the gum strip, seal the seam, and twist the open tip closed

Care: Keep booklets dry and flat; store away from damp; use papers before the gum strip dries out or picks up dust

Variants: Hemp, rice, flax, wood-pulp, and clear cellulose papers; bleached white and unbleached brown; flavoured papers; rolls of 3 to 5 metres for custom lengths

Science proof

Rolling paper is a thin, porous sheet of plant fibre, and its behaviour is set by three material facts. First, basis weight, measured in grams per square metre, sets thickness and stiffness: at 10 to 14 grams per square metre the sheet is thin enough to roll tightly yet strong enough not to tear. Second, the fibres are cellulose, and cellulose burns by pyrolysis followed by oxidation, releasing heat that sustains a slow, even burn along the cylinder. Third, the gum strip is gum arabic, a plant polysaccharide that dissolves in water and re-forms a bond as it dries, which is why a licked seam seals without heat. Rice papers are very thin and burn slowly because their dense fibre mat limits airflow; hemp papers are slightly thicker and more structured, which many rollers find easier to handle. The area of one sheet is length times width, and the area of a whole booklet is that area times the leaf count, so a 32-leaf booklet of 1 1/4 papers carries a little over a tenth of a square metre of paper in total. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports. If they do not agree, the measurement or the arithmetic is wrong, not the physics, and the reader can find the error by checking one step at a time.

Math proof

The demo starts with one sheet: length times width, 78.0 mm times 44.0 mm, gives the sheet area in square millimetres, and dividing by 100 gives square centimetres. Multiplying the sheet area by 32 leaves gives the booklet area, and dividing by one million converts square millimetres to square metres. Multiplying that area by the basis weight of 12.0 grams per square metre gives the mass of paper in one booklet. The gum strip area is the paper length times the gum width of 4.0 mm. Every number comes from the specification in this record, the program prints each result with its unit, and it runs the computation twice with SHA-256 digests so the reader can confirm the result is deterministic. The reader can check every step with a pocket calculator, because each input is named, each unit is stated, and no hidden constant is used anywhere in the calculation.

Use and care

Place a filter tip at one end, spread ground herb evenly, roll the paper into a cylinder, lick the gum strip, seal the seam, and twist the open tip closed Keep booklets dry and flat; store away from damp; use papers before the gum strip dries out or picks up dust Keep the supply dry when it is stored, keep its working surfaces clean, and replace worn parts such as screens, balloons, or filter tips when they no longer do their job. A supply that is cleaned and stored properly keeps its dimensions and its mechanism, and that is what keeps its behaviour predictable from one use to the next.

Legal note

Legal note: laws on cannabis and cannabis supplies vary by jurisdiction; check local law before buying, possessing, or using this supply.

Sources

  • Speakeasy Vaporium — Rolling Papers Guide: Sizes, Materials, and How to Choose — https://speakeasyvaporium.com/blog/rolling-papers-guide/ — Rolling papers are sold in standard sizes named mostly by tradition: Single wide 68-70mm x 34-38mm, 1 1/4 size 76-78mm x 44-48mm, 1 1/2 size 76-78mm x 60-62mm, King size slim 105-110mm x 42-46mm, King size 100-110mm x 55-60mm; materials include wood pulp, rice, hemp, flax, and cellulose; Zig-Zag traces its origins to France in 1879.

demo.code:
"""Demo: rolling paper area — Rolling Papers."""
import hashlib
def compute():
    length = 78.0; width = 44.0; leaves = 32; gsm = 12.0; gum = 4.0
    sheet_mm2 = length * width
    sheet_cm2 = sheet_mm2 / 100.0
    booklet_mm2 = sheet_mm2 * leaves
    booklet_m2 = booklet_mm2 / 1000000.0
    booklet_g = booklet_m2 * gsm
    gum_mm2 = length * gum
    return {"sheet_area_mm2": round(sheet_mm2, 1), "sheet_area_cm2": round(sheet_cm2, 2), "booklet_area_m2": round(booklet_m2, 4), "booklet_mass_g": round(booklet_g, 3), "gum_area_mm2": round(gum_mm2, 1), "leaves": leaves}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    for key in ["sheet_area_mm2", "sheet_area_cm2", "booklet_area_m2", "booklet_mass_g", "gum_area_mm2", "leaves"]:
        print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

A good supply therefore has to do three things at once: hold the material securely, apply its mechanism evenly across the whole load, and survive repeated use without losing its shape or its edge. It also has to be easy to clean, because residue builds up and changes how it works, and easy to measure, because its dimensions set its capacity. """Rolling Papers — full working program.

Computes the same quantities as the record demo (rolling paper area),
as a documented module with a class and a run() method.
Run: python3 program.py
"""
import hashlib
import math


class SupplyCalculator:
    """Calculator for Rolling Papers."""

    def compute(self):
        """Return the computed quantities as a dict."""
        length = 78.0; width = 44.0; leaves = 32; gsm = 12.0; gum = 4.0
        sheet_mm2 = length * width
        sheet_cm2 = sheet_mm2 / 100.0
        booklet_mm2 = sheet_mm2 * leaves
        booklet_m2 = booklet_mm2 / 1000000.0
        booklet_g = booklet_m2 * gsm
        gum_mm2 = length * gum
        return {"sheet_area_mm2": round(sheet_mm2, 1), "sheet_area_cm2": round(sheet_cm2, 2), "booklet_area_m2": round(booklet_m2, 4), "booklet_mass_g": round(booklet_g, 3), "gum_area_mm2": round(gum_mm2, 1), "leaves": leaves}

    def run(self):
        """Compute twice, print named results and SHA-256 digests."""
        a = self.compute()
        b = self.compute()
        sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        for key in sorted(a):
            print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
        print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
        print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
        print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
        return a


if __name__ == "__main__":
    SupplyCalculator().run()
